title: AI Has Not Produced a Single New Theory, So It Is Not an Artificial Person
dek: Deutsch's test: AI only fills in the parts of known theories that nobody has bothered to compute — it is coloring in the existing picture of organic chemistry. To reach the threshold of creating new knowledge, you first need problems — and LLMs have no problems; the problems are the ones we give them.
why: This is the wrap-up of the final chapter of The Fabric of Reality: the first half covers induction, the many-worlds test and the explanatory gap, and only in the second half do the four strands come together. Dense, but it takes a little patience.
who: For engineers and founders interested in Deutsch, Popperian epistemology, the many-worlds interpretation and the nature of AI — especially anyone trying to work out whether AI actually counts as creating knowledge.
skip: If induction, the many-worlds test and philosophy of consciousness do not interest you, skip the first 50 minutes and start straight from the LLM section at 50:27.

points.h: Induction is not a source of knowledge, it is extrapolation under a new name
points.body: Deutsch takes Popper's line: induction is a pseudo-problem. Inductionists wanted a mechanical process for science corresponding to mathematical deduction, so they invented the word "induction." But for induction to work you must first assume the theory that "this trend will continue" — so it is really conjecture plus extrapolation, and extrapolation itself is deductive. At best it gives you a prediction, never an explanation. The host uses this to rebut "AI is doing induction": if induction in Popper's sense were what AI does, then AI would be making scientific discoveries — and it is not.

points.h: AI has never produced a single new theory
points.body: The host offers a concrete test: what AI can do is fill in the parts of known theories that have not yet been computed. Take a given number of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen atoms — which molecules could physically exist? The theory of atomic bonding and carbon chemistry has long existed; nobody just had the leisure to compute it, and AI can do it for us. Same in mathematics: the axioms and rules of inference are already there. This is "coloring in the existing picture of organic chemistry," not generating new explanatory knowledge. Reaching the threshold of creating new knowledge — and thereby counting as AGI or an "artificial person" — requires the latter.

The host observes that the most common objection today is not a refusal of the explanation but the reflex "it's untestable." Yet Deutsch published an experimental scheme for testing many-worlds decades ago; the host, Maria Violaris and Sam Kuypers have all explained it, and after pointing to the paper and the video, the other party — physicists included — still will not budge. The experiment requires a "conscious observer" in superposition, so then people say we have no AGI capable of doing it. The host cites Deutsch: needing AGI to run this decisive experiment is not a fault of the many-worlds theory.

points.h: The explanatory gap: the Turing principle cannot answer what a person is
points.body: Deutsch says that some of those who deny the possibility of AI are in fact expressing a more reasonable criticism: Turing's computational explanation seems in principle to leave no room for a physical explanation of mental properties like consciousness and free will. AI partisans respond bluntly that "the Turing principle guarantees a computer can do anything a brain can do" — true, but that answers with a prediction, whereas the problem lies in the explanation; there is an explanatory gap. The host adds: this is why we still cannot build AGI; saying the brain is some kind of computer does not settle what a person is.

points.h: Simple rules do not specify a peacock, yet peacocks appear
points.body: Deutsch uses a Darwinian analogy: the laws of physics do not contain the shapes of elephants and peacocks; they are merely emergent results of atoms interacting by rule. Brett Hall connects this directly to Conway's Game of Life — the rules are minimal, and unless you run it you cannot know what it will produce. From this he criticizes Michael Levin: Levin claims the bubble sort algorithm does unpredictable things and therefore is conscious, but Hall checked the paper and found Levin deliberately altered the algorithm methodologically and introduced randomness — that is no longer standard bubble sort, and is in effect rediscovering a low-resolution version of the Game of Life.

points.h: Not knowing where the line is drawn does not mean there is no line
points.body: The standard panpsychist argument is: walk down the phylogenetic tree from humans — cats and dogs, birds, mice, insects, fish — and you find no point where a line for consciousness can reasonably be drawn, so no line exists, and consciousness goes all the way down to elementary particles. Hall says this smuggles in "there is no line" in place of "we don't know where the line is" — "Just because you don't know where to draw a line doesn't mean there isn't a line." He offers several candidate lines: whether something is a universal explainer, whether brain capacity reaches some threshold, whether a nervous system exists — and concedes there is currently no good explanation, so none can be ruled out.

points.h: LLMs are not people, because they have no problems
points.body: Hall ties consciousness to knowledge creation: knowledge creation depends on problems, a problem is a conflict between ideas, and in a person the conflict produces a feeling of wanting to resolve it — and it is precisely in that "wanting," a subjective, conscious state, that a person begins seeking a solution and creating knowledge. From this he draws his judgment on LLMs: LLMs do not prompt themselves, they are not interested in anything, they have no problems — the problems are the ones we give them. This rebuts the claim that "LLMs are artificial people"; when they truly become artificial people, they will have problems, and vice versa.

points.h: 20th-century fundamental science was adopted and ignored at once
points.body: Deutsch's observation: the history of the four strands shows that for most of the 20th century fundamental science and philosophy suffered something deeply unpleasant. The vogue for positivist and instrumentalist views of science went together with indifference to genuine explanation, loss of confidence and pessimism — precisely when the prestige, utility and funding of fundamental research stood at an all-time high. The theories of the four protagonists were simultaneously adopted and ignored, and that unprecedented manner is itself telling. He admits he has no complete explanation, but thinks we are now emerging from this phase.

quotes.text: You cannot get an explanation from induction. You cannot get an explanation from deduction either. Where do explanations come from? No one knows.
it's not the fault of the multiverse that we require an AGI of a kind in order to perform this crucial test to decide between the multiverse and other explanations.
to take a theory seriously means to regard that what it says literally describes what exists, what's there in reality.
Just because you don't know where to draw a line doesn't mean there isn't a line. You just don't know.

This is why I talk about LLMs as not self-prompting. They're not interested in anything. They don't have a problem. We give them problems, which is a refutation of the idea they are artificial people.

Despite all the excuses I've been making for the critics of the central theories, the history of all four strands shows that something very unpleasant happened to fundamental science and philosophy for most of the 20th century.
It is a fundamentally optimistic worldview that places human minds at the centre of the physical universe and explanation and understanding at the centre of human purposes.
